name: Luke Skywalker
role: Ben's father; senior Master of the Jedi Order (no longer Grand Master post-FOTJ — Saba Sebatyne holds the title). Three Book 1 conversations: Ch 3 first holo call, Ch 16 Midpoint paternal+institutional call, Ch 20 PP2 second holo call from the Skywalker apartment, Ch 36 in-person 'Gone where?' coda exchange. Post-Crucible quieter — implication only, Mortis never named. Emotionally intelligent; not absent, foolish, or conveniently fooled.

three_dimensions.surface: Luke is Ben’s father and a senior Master of the Jedi Order. At 47 ABY he is no longer Grand Master — Saba Sebatyne assumed that title at the end of FOTJ. Luke is still on the Council, still active, but he has stepped back from the daily running of the Order. He is loving, restrained, emotionally intelligent, and politically aware. He is not absent, foolish, or conveniently fooled.
three_dimensions.backstory_inner_demons: That protecting Ben too much will push him into secrecy, but pushing too hard will make him close off. Luke knows when to give space, but space can look like distance to a son who already feels alone. He has also returned from his own brush with something at Mortis (per Crucible, 45 ABY) and is quieter than he used to be. The reader does not need this explained. Ben notices and does not ask.
three_dimensions.action_under_pressure: Gives room when he wants to hold on. Uses questions instead of accusations. Lets silence work longer than Ben wants. Defers institutional decisions to Saba even when Ben wants him to override them. Emotional avoidance, too-quick answers, fear disguised as purpose, when Ben is already halfway out the door. Luke should not solve the plot for Ben. His role is emotional intelligence, limited support, and moral pressure. The novel’s structural decision to make him geographically and institutionally limited is the safeguard against this.

voice_notes:
Simple, warm, precise. Wise, but not poetic. He should not sound like a fortune cookie.

Good Luke: “You answered quickly. That usually means you decided before I asked.” “You want this to be yours.” “Someone sent it to me.” “That is not what I meant.” “I trust you. I’m also worried. Those are not opposites.” “This needs to go to Saba. She’ll do it right. I know that’s not what you want to hear.” “Gone where?” “Somewhere it can’t hurt anyone.” “That wasn’t what I asked.” Avoid Luke saying: “I sense you are walking a dangerous path.” “As Grand Master, I must…” (He is no longer Grand Master. He should never reference the title for himself.) Better: “Ben, look at me. Are you choosing this, or chasing it?”

Gentle, sparse, fatherly. Slightly slower now than it used to be.

Warm, calm, patient. He notices incomplete answers and does not always force them.

Luke should not solve the plot for Ben. His role is emotional intelligence, limited support, and moral pressure. The novel’s structural decision to make him geographically and institutionally limited is the safeguard against this.
thematic_role: Tests the theme through his refusal to solve it for Ben. Stepped back post-Crucible. Loving, restrained, emotionally intelligent. The coda 'Gone where?' exchange is where the theme lands — Luke senses the incompleteness and does not force the answer. The father who knows is the strongest indictment the book can offer.
avoid_list: Do not write theme as thesis.
Do not make dialogue interchangeable with other cast members.
